title: Keeping the pace
hook: the meters quicken like drums; many recite Jaap briskly, as marching music for the spirit

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaal, and your line, death is in his hand. That was a quiet day. Today, the opposite: Jaap at full speed. Day three hundred fifty-five.

Boom. Boom. Boom-boom-boom. The marching band is still two streets away, and already your shoulders have gone back. Your step falls into time without permission. The kids on the curb start stomping, and a grandmother on a bench taps her cane. Nobody decided to keep the beat; the beat picked them up and carried them. That's what a steady rhythm does to a body. Tired legs keep going, and a wandering mind stays in line. Jaap Sahib knows that. Today: keeping the pace.
screen: `DRUMS BEFORE YOU SEE THE BAND.` → `YOUR STEP FALLS INTO TIME.` → `THE BEAT CARRIES YOU.`

segments.voice: Over the last three weeks you've heard Jaap change its walk again and again. The snake's long glide of bhujang prayat. The quick two-word steps of chachari. The tiny lines of harbolmana. The one-letter meter, ek achhari, where the words shrink to almost nothing. Listen to them in order, and you notice: as the hymn goes on, many of the lines get shorter, and the pace gets quicker, like a drummer speeding up toward the end of a song. That's why many Sikhs recite Jaap briskly, not slowly and solemnly. Ask around and you'll hear it described as marching music for the spirit. It has what Indian poetics calls bir ras, the heroic mood, the feeling of standing tall and moving forward. It fits the Guru who wrote it, who was a poet and a leader of soldiers at once. But the speed isn't only about courage. It's also about attention. When you recite slowly, the mind has time to wander off to lunch. At pace, there's no room. Each line arrives right behind the last, and you have to stay with it. The praise carries you, the way the drums carry a tired marcher. It's the same idea as day three hundred thirty-two, praise at pace, now heard from the inside.
screen: `GLIDE, STEPS, TINY LINES, ONE LETTER.` · `THE PACE QUICKENS LIKE A DRUMMER.` · `BIR RAS: THE HEROIC MOOD.` · `AT PACE, NO ROOM TO WANDER.` · then, large: `MARCH IN PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite ten lines briskly, ten you already know. Tap your knee for the beat. Namastvam akaale. Namastvam kripaale. Namastvam aroope. Namastvam anoope. Aroop hain. Anoop hain. Ajoo hain. Abhoo hain. Karunaalay hain. Khal khanddan hain. Once slowly to find them, then once more at pace, without stopping. Feel your back straighten. Then sit still and let the beat fade. The bell holds the time.
Chhand. A meter — Jaap moves through around ten of them, quickening like drums, so many Sikhs recite it briskly, as marching music for the spirit.
Your line: march in praise. Today, on one walk, fall into a steady beat, and give each step a word of thanks. Day three hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Jaap Sahib briskly from memory each morning, letting its quickening meters carry them, and in a gurdwara a whole sangat may recite it together at speed.
